descriptors.R: nominee of the party of the administration in office since 1897
descriptors.D: nominee of the party that has held a majority in the House since the 1910 elections
descriptors.O: former President, nominee of a new party of progressive insurgents who bolted the convention of the party in office

compile_desc.R: the party of the administration in office since 1897
compile_desc.D: the party that has held a majority in the House since the 1910 elections

others_line: Other candidates on some ballots, including a Socialist, a Prohibition and a Socialist Labor nominee (answer "other").
never_name: Taft, Wilson, Roosevelt, Sherman, Marshall, Johnson, Debs, Bryan, Champ Clark or La Follette

slice_sources.men: 1910 and 1920 censuses interpolated to November 1912; men 21+ outside the eleven Southern states (including declarant aliens where they could vote); turnout and choice from the backbone, calibrated to certified 1912 returns.
slice_sources.women: 1910 and 1920 censuses interpolated to November 1912; women 21+ outside the South; women could vote for president only in Wyoming, Colorado, Utah, Idaho, Washington (1910) and California (1911); Arizona, Kansas and Oregon adopted suffrage at this same election, so their women first voted for president in 1916.
slice_sources.south-white: 1910 and 1920 censuses interpolated to November 1912; white adults in the eleven former Confederate states (includes a small number of American Indian and Asian adults); calibrated to certified 1912 returns.
slice_sources.black-south: 1910 and 1920 censuses interpolated to November 1912; Black adults in the eleven former Confederate states; disfranchisement by poll tax, literacy test, grandfather clause and white primary was near complete across the region; the shortfall against white turnout is counted as exclusion.
slice_sources.immigrants: 1910 and 1920 censuses interpolated to November 1912; foreign-born white adults who were aliens or had only declared their intent (first papers); declarant aliens could vote in several Midwestern and Western states (fewer each decade as states repealed it), so part of this slice could vote.
